description: We’re a Uruguayan team from Universidad Católica del Uruguay. For this year’s NASA Space Apps Challenge, we worked on the harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS hotspots and created EmberCast, a web app that merges the two satellite fire records into one reliable history and turns it into a clear 7-day fire risk brief. Since fire season matters in both Uruguay and California, we built EmberCast for both regions, available in English and Spanish.
summary:
MODIS and VIIRS have tracked active fires for more than two decades, but their records cannot be compared directly: add them together and fire seems to triple in 2012, when VIIRS comes online. EmberCast harmonizes both sensors into one daily burn-activity record, validated on years the calibration never saw (annual cross-sensor error falls from 62% to 14% in Uruguay and from 48% to 9% in California), and turns it into a burn calendar and a 7-day fire risk brief per zone that is already interpreted and always verifiable. 

It matters because the people who prevent fires, and anyone planning around them, need a trustworthy history and a clear answer, not a map they have to interpret themselves.
details:
EmberCast turns two incompatible satellite fire records into one reliable record, and then into a fire risk brief that people can act on.

What it does. For each zone, the web app delivers a brief, not a map: a risk level for the next 7 days, the reasons behind it, how current activity compares with 25 years of history, and how much to trust it. One click away is the evidence: a map with the real MODIS and VIIRS detections and a replay of what happened next, and a burn calendar for 2001–2025 with anomalies, the critical period of the year and CSV download. A planner lets anyone check a trip, an outdoor event, field or industrial work, or a prescribed burn, and proposes safer dates and places. An alert flow shows how the brief would reach a subscriber. It works in English and Spanish, for two regions: Uruguay (19 departments) and California (58 counties).

How it works. MODIS (since 2000, about 1 km pixels) and VIIRS (since 2012, 375 m pixels) see the same fire differently: one MODIS detection is often several VIIRS detections, and VIIRS also sees smaller fires. A detection is an observation, not a fire, so the two counts are never added. We harmonize them in four steps:

  1. Common schema: the same columns and one confidence scale, dropping low-confidence detections and non-vegetation sources.
  2. Common grid and day: we count active 1 km cells per day, not detections.
  3. Calibration on the shared years (2012–2025): per zone we measure how much more activity VIIRS registers than MODIS, shrinking noisy zones toward the regional factor. A separate factor covers the Terra-only months before Aqua.
  4. Output: a daily activity index per zone in VIIRS-equivalent active cells, flagged with the sensors that observed it and an uncertainty band before 2012.

Does it hold? We fitted the factor on 2012–2018 only and checked it on 2019–2025, years the fit never saw. In Uruguay the annual MODIS–VIIRS error drops from 62% to 14% and the monthly correlation is r = 0.98 (factor ×2.40, ±15% by year). In California it drops from 48% to 9%, with r = 0.99 (factor ×1.90). The app shows a real fire seen by both sensors on the same day: 2 MODIS detections against 8 VIIRS detections become 2 and 3 active cells.

What is real and what is not. The fire record, the harmonization, the calendar, the map detections and the globe on the landing page are real NASA data and real computation. The 7-day risk levels, their reasons and the model metrics are illustrative: generated with a fixed seed on top of the real record, using only information available on the issue date, and labelled "Illustrative" throughout the app. The next step is a LightGBM model trained on 2012–2022, tuned on 2023 and tested on 2024–2025 against seasonal history, persistence, logistic regression and a weather-only fire index, scored with precision-recall rather than plain accuracy.

Benefits and goals. Emergency coordinators, firefighters and park rangers get a ranked list of their zones with reasons, so crews, permits and warnings are ready before conditions peak. Travellers, event organisers and field operations get a clear verdict and safer alternatives. Responders, land managers and scientists get one comparable 25-year record to see how unusual today is and to review what happened. When MODIS retires, the series continues with VIIRS without a break.

Known limits. It cannot recover small fires MODIS never saw (it estimates them on average); it does not correct overpass times; satellites cannot see through clouds; 2000–2002 is Terra-only and less reliable; this version uses VIIRS S-NPP only. Risk means probability of satellite-detectable fire activity in a ~25 km cell: it is not a real-time alert and does not replace official warning systems.

Tools. Data pipeline: Python and NumPy. Web app: React, Vite and TypeScript, static, hosted on GitHub Pages. Where to find it. Live site: https://embercast.earth (direct link, if the domain is not reachable: https://pauxan707.github.io/EmberCast-NASA-Space-Apps/). Source code: https://github.com/pauxan707/EmberCast-NASA-Space-Apps
